details:
Helios is an iPhone and iPad app that acts as a personal flight surgeon for astronauts on long missions. It syncs continuously with Apple Health and Apple Watch, reading heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen, blood pressure, activity and symptoms. It also accepts manual measurements, a one-minute daily check-in, and live data from a radiation detector. The app learns each person's own normal values and flags meaningful changes as OK, Watch, Act or Escalate, explaining each change in plain language with the numbers behind it. Results appear on an interactive body map and across NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. A radiation module detects solar-particle spikes, tracks the total dose and guides the crew to shelter. Crews get clear next steps, are told when to contact the flight surgeon, and can export a report for them.

On the way to Mars, a message to Earth can take over 20 minutes each way, so crews need to spot and act on health problems themselves. Helios gives them that independence using devices they already wear. Comparing people with their own normal values instead of averages reduces false alarms and catches subtle changes. Everything runs offline and stays on the device. We made health visual with a body map instead of a single score. We also built a 180-day mission simulator so anyone can watch problems appear and get caught in minutes.

We built Helios in Swift and SwiftUI with Apple's HealthKit, Swift Charts and SQLite, and tested it on the iOS Simulator. The radiation bridge is written in Python and works with consumer Geiger counters or a simulated source. We used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to help write and test the code. Our main concerns were safety, privacy and honesty. Helios is decision support, not a medical device, and urgent alerts are never downgraded. There are no accounts or servers, and sharing with crewmates is opt-in. Simulated data and unreviewed guidance are clearly labelled.
projectRefs: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health (Canadian Space Agency)
